message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for drawing images, now also for highly parallel compute tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) optimized for low latency, complex control flow, and large caches. | Hundreds to thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput and SIMD (single instruction, multiple data). |
| **Instruction set** | Complex, capable of branching, recursion, and varied operations. | Simple, repetitive, often SIMD-friendly. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on massive bandwidth from shared memory. |
| **Typical workloads** | Sequential tasks, decision making, I/O, small data sets. | Data‑parallel tasks: matrix multiplication, image/video processing, machine learning inference/training, scientific simulations. |
| **Performance characteristics** | Low latency, high single‑thread performance. | High throughput, low latency only when many threads run simultaneously. |
| **Energy efficiency** | Optimized for a mix of performance and power; each core consumes more power. | Optimized for throughput per watt; many cores share power budget. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional CPU programming (C/C++, Java, etc.) with multi‑threading. | Requires parallel programming frameworks (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan, Metal, DirectX 12). |

In short, a CPU is great for “doing one thing well” and handling diverse tasks, while a GPU excels at “doing many things the same way” in parallel. Modern systems often combine both: the CPU handles control flow and general tasks, and the GPU accelerates compute‑heavy, data‑parallel workloads.
